papers.title: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds
papers.authors: Matteo Agius-D', Zachary Zelner, Harrison Ju, Rushab Munot Arrigo
papers.abstract: Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.
papers.summary: Applications often need a count of how many filtered records meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as why a patient stopped a drug, and they need that count in seconds before starting a batch pipeline. Prior systems have an expensive model label a sample at query time, so every query waits. The new system calibrates a fast classifier offline from logs of the production judge and does not call that judge at query time. It samples at most a thousand records, then multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact filtered count. In a multi-tenant production deployment, p99 latency is 3.8 seconds; on tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the pipeline count in 92% of estimates, though the estimates run about 15% high in aggregate.

papers.title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
papers.abstract: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.
papers.summary: A four-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware, so existing kernels have to decode the values in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 path is up to 1.7 times slower than FP8 and uses only a small fraction of memory bandwidth. The new decode kernel overlaps loads with compute and lays the cache out at write time so decoded values can enter the tensor cores from registers. Inside vLLM, on a mid-size Llama 3.1 model at moderate batches, it decodes 1.12 to 1.64 times faster per step than FlashInfer's FP8 path and holds substantially more tokens. On five mid-size models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV.

papers.title: Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Building a Template-Driven ML Ecosystem
papers.authors: Anirudh Agrawal, Djordje Gligorijevic, Yao Xuan, Peggy Yao, Jiang Liu, John Martabano Landy, Rahul Suresh
papers.abstract: In practice, we use a small set of templates that cover major ranking and retrieval patterns across different model sizes.
papers.summary: In a large ranking and retrieval fleet, trying a new technique on every model separately piles engineering time into repeated work. Meta uses a small set of templates that cover the main ranking and retrieval patterns, so a mature change can be designed once and rolled out across models of different sizes. Over the last two years, that cut per-model engineering time by 92%, improved offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift. Models that adopt a mature template also inherit a history of generalized improvements instead of starting from an isolated baseline.

papers.title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
papers.abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.
papers.summary: Exact nearest-neighbor search usually either scans the whole dataset or falls back to approximate neighbors, and recent half-precision proofs that skip most vectors still expect one GPU to hold the entire set. The new system keeps only the short proof rows in GPU memory and fetches the remaining full vectors from host memory, so it can answer Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it finishes 10,000 exact queries over a billion vectors in 1.1 seconds, instead of five minutes for exhaustive search. On several open language models, retrieving the exact top-10 attention keys is 2.2 to 13.1 times faster than exhaustive search.

papers.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
papers.abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.
papers.summary: Serving teams often turn on prefix caching, chunked prefill, or speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents these features as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. The authors serve one mid-size instruction model and grade about three thousand requests under nine single-feature configurations. With default kernels, the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% to 1.78% of requests, none above the 1.72% floor from reordering the same requests. An FP8 KV cache flips 3.36%. Under batch-invariant kernels, those seven features reproduce the reference text on every request, but the FP8 KV cache still flips answers.

papers.title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xin Zhang, Weifeng Zhang, Xianyan Xie, Huijun Shen, Xijin Yin, Zhen He, Yinben Xia, Xiang Li, ZeKun He, Yachen Wang, Xianneng Zou, Guo Chen
papers.abstract: Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer. We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets. We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K--64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65--0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28--23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08--1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.
papers.summary: After attention data is offloaded, long-context sparse-attention serving can still be limited by GPU memory, because Indexer-K state used to pick tokens keeps growing. The new runtime stages completed pages through shared buffers, keeps new entries local, and checks storage and transfer budgets before growing the batch, while leaving the native score, top-k, and attention kernels in place. On sixteen model-serving GPUs and sixteen backing H800 GPUs, batch size rises 12.28% to 23.08% over host-memory-backed HiSparse. Decode throughput reaches 1.08 to 1.14 times. Mixed-length dynamic serving also raises the mean generating batch and decode throughput.

papers.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
papers.abstract: Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.
papers.summary: Under structured outputs, speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation. The new method treats the grammar as a second drafter: before verification it merges forced tokens with the proposal into one row, skips logits for grammar-determined positions, and adds no new kernels on the critical path. On a JSON character-profile benchmark on TPUs, MTP with a smaller Qwen3.5 model raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43. Single-request decoding is 2.66 to 2.81 times faster, with a narrower gain at large batches.

papers.title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Mohammad Mahdi Moradi, Ali Pourranjbar, Zongzuo Wang, Mingming Zhu, Ben Feng, Boxing Chen
papers.abstract: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.
papers.summary: Parallel speculative decoders propose a whole token block at once, so one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject the rest of the suffix. The new method lets each candidate attend to earlier choices in the block, precomputes those interactions as table lookups so inference does not repeat a neural pass, and trains the shared backbone with an autoregressive loss on clean prefixes. Across eight math, code, and dialogue benchmarks with mid-size Qwen3 targets, it commits 13% to 15% more tokens per verification round than DSpark. Mean speedups reach 3.35 times and 3.37 times under greedy decoding. Higher acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding, because the cost of each round still matters.

papers.title: Training Transformers for KV-Cache Compressibility
papers.authors: Yoav Gelberg, Yam Eitan, Michael M. Bronstein, Yarin Gal, Haggai Maron
papers.abstract: Long-context language modeling is increasingly constrained by the Key–Value (KV) cache, whose memory and decode-time access costs scale linearly with the prefix length. This bottleneck has motivated a range of context-compression methods, from token-level summarization to recent optimization-based KV compression methods. These post-hoc methods operate on the KV cache of a fixed pretrained model, so their effectiveness is fundamentally limited by how well the model's internal representations can be compressed. In this work, we formalize the notion of KV compressibility and show that it is a property of the *learned representations*, rather than of the context alone. We prove that almost any sequence-to-vector function admits both highly compressible and inherently non-compressible transformer implementations, highlighting the need to guide transformers toward compressible representations during training. Motivated by this, we propose **KV**-**C**ompression **A**ware **T**raining (KV-CAT), a continued pretraining procedure that incentivizes the emergence of compressible representations. We introduce a train-time KV sparsification policy that masks KV slots during training. This forces the model to use fewer KV slots and encourages it to learn representations amenable to post-hoc compression. Empirically, we show that KV-CAT improves the quality–budget tradeoff of downstream compression methods across retrieval, long-context question answering, and perplexity-based evaluation of compressed-prefix continuation.
papers.summary: How well a KV cache can be compressed after training depends on the learned representations, not only on the context itself. The paper proves that almost any sequence-to-vector function admits both a highly compressible Transformer implementation and one that is inherently hard to compress. The new continued-pretraining procedure masks KV slots during training, forcing the model to use fewer slots and to learn representations that later compression can exploit. On open base models, that improves the quality-budget tradeoff of downstream compression, by up to 3.21 times in suffix perplexity retention, 68% in retrieval accuracy, and 39% in long-context question answering.

papers.title: PatchKV: Weight Space Compensation of KV Cache
papers.authors: Chanryeol Lee, Chanhyuk Lee, Yeonwoo Choi, Donggyun Kim, Seunghoon Hong
papers.abstract: Long-context inference with Large Language Models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by the linearly growing memory of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing compression methods reduce the cache through token eviction or approximation, but degrade sharply at aggressive compression budgets. We propose PatchKV, a training-free framework that compensates KV cache compression methods by carrying part of the context in the model's weights. PatchKV pairs an off-the-shelf compressed KV cache with a context-specific weight patch, which is computed once at context-loading time and served for downstream queries for the context. The weight patch is derived in closed form via ridge regression, by aligning the block-wise activations of context-derived reference query tokens under the full cache and the compressed cache. Once merged into the model, the patch leaves the forward graph and per-query inference cost unchanged in the single-context, multi-query setting. Across long-context QA (SCBench with up to 170k tokens, SQuAD, NIAH) and math (GSM8K) benchmarks on three model architectures, PatchKV consistently improves cache compression methods, suggesting an alternative direction to compensate them at aggressive budgets.
papers.summary: During long-context inference the KV cache grows linearly with the prefix, and existing compression methods degrade sharply at aggressive budgets. The new method needs no extra training: at context-loading time it computes a weight patch in closed form, carrying part of the dropped context in the model weights, then leaves the forward graph and per-query cost unchanged for later queries on the same context. Across SCBench, SQuAD, NIAH, and GSM8K, and on three model architectures, it improves off-the-shelf cache compression, especially at budgets below one fifth of the full cache, and recovers a substantial fraction of the accuracy gap.

scenario: Today's infrastructure papers ask how serving can use less GPU memory and less waiting, without quietly changing answers. Some turn semantic counts into a seconds-scale approximation that no longer calls an expensive model at query time. Some rewrite 4-bit cache decoding on Hopper, or stage indexer state across memory tiers. Exact nearest neighbors can finish over a billion vectors in seconds, while serving features documented as exact can still flip which requests are graded correctly. Structured output treats the grammar as a drafter, and parallel speculation adds prefix information inside a token block. Work on compressing the KV cache comes from both training more compressible representations and patching the weights after compression.
